[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — uh — appreciate you taking the time. Quick intro, I'm Jordan, AE at Redwood Inference, and with me is Priya our solutions eng.

[00:52] Samir Patel: sure. For risk scoring, it's synchronous API called from transaction pipeline. Average QPS is 25 during peak hour, but bursts to ~200 QPS for a few minutes during batch ingests. Concurrency per instance is more like 40-50. Payloads are small: ~50 tokens in, ~30 tokens out.
[01:15] Jordan Lee: ok small token footprints there, good for batching. And the conversational assistant?
[01:20] Samir Patel: that's lower QPS, peak 5-10 QPS, but much bigger context windows — we see average input tokens 400, responses 300, with a heavy tail up to 2k tokens for long threads.
[01:33] Lena Ortiz: the assistant is for internal ops, so latency target is 1.5s for 95th for scoring and 4s p95 for chat is acceptable. Cost target is the other side — we want to be under our current bill which is rough estimate of $0.015 per request for scoring.

[01:50] Priya Raman: got it. For the pilot we usually run two benches: a latency bench (p95/p99) and a throughput bench (sustained QPS and burst handling). We'll need a sample of your prompt set and a traffic CSV that shows timestamped reqs ideally over a week.
[02:06] Samir Patel: we can provide a 24-72 hour sample and synthetic bursts. We'll also include the real prompts for top 100 flows.
[02:14] Jordan Lee: perfect. Success criteria — can you share how you define "pass" for the POC?
[02:20] Samir Patel: pass means two things: 1) p95 latency under 1.5s for scoring at our normal traffic and handling bursts up to 200 QPS with graceful degradation, and 2) chat answers maintain quality similar to current baseline (we'll provide evaluation prompts and acceptable thresholds). If both pass, we'll talk about dedicated capacity.
[02:37] Priya Raman: when you say graceful degradation, do you prefer fallback to a cheaper model, or queued requests with higher latency?
[02:44] Marco Ruiz: fallback is fine as long as it's deterministic — we can't have hallucinations. We'd prefer a quantized model variant if possible.
[02:51] Priya Raman: Redwood supports policy-based routing — you can route by cost/latency and fallback to compatible model variants. Note our runtime has prefix/KV cache — sometimes transcribed as KV cash in notes — it helps with repeated context.

[03:05] Lena Ortiz: security stuff — do you support customer-managed KMS, SSO, audit logs retention? We need SOC2 type II and enterprise key management.
[03:13] Jordan Lee: yes, we have Private deployment options with customer-managed KMS/HSM and audit logs. We'll share SOC2 cert and typical architecture doc. For a quick pilot you can use our hosted API with VPC peering and log forwarding. We'll attach the security pack.

[03:30] Priya Raman: back to workload modeling — two important distributions we model: input token distribution and output token distribution. For scoring it's narrow (50 in / 30 out) so batching is effective; for chat it's wide-tailed which affects memory and KV cache.
[03:44] Samir Patel: can you simulate our tail? We get occasional 2k-token replies.
[03:48] Priya Raman: yes, we can include tail heavy samples in the benchmark; that will surface kernel selection differences and possibly require different instance types or longer seq-length configs.

[04:00] Jordan Lee: what about concurrency targets — do you want dedicated pool sizing or dynamic scaling?

[04:18] Priya Raman: we usually map QPS to concurrent tokens/sec and model latency to compute GPU seconds. For example, a 25 QPS scoring workload with 50-in/30-out tokens at 95th latency 300ms maps to about X GPU cores; we'll run automated capacity modeling.
[04:33] Samir Patel: can you show a worked example in the report? Our finance team wants cost per 1M requests at p95 latency.
[04:40] Jordan Lee: absolutely. We'll provide a cost model: per-token cost estimates, batching efficiency assumptions, and sensitivity analysis (latency vs cost).

[04:50] Priya Raman: benchmarking approach — we'll run baseline on Redwood-hosted with recommended model variants. We'll measure p50/p95/p99 latencies, throughput (sustained and burst), and token-level cost. We'll also run an experiment enabling KV caching and then without to quantify benefit.
[05:05] Lena Ortiz: what tooling do you use? We currently have Locust for load and a custom harness.
[05:10] Priya Raman: we can integrate with your Locust harness or run our internal bench. For reproducibility we'll store the test config and scripts in a shared repo. We'll also provide raw logs and an analysis sheet (link will be shared).

[05:29] Priya Raman: we'll recommend two variants: a lower-cost quantized variant for scoring, and a higher-accuracy variant for chat. We'll also include suggestions for sequence-length tuned kernels.
